x: CUBE finds and measures behaviour in video of animals. It combines DeepLabCut (DLC) pose estimation with unsupervised machine learning: it tracks body points, groups similar movements into clusters, lets you name the clusters by watching example clips, and then compares behaviour between animals or groups. The method builds on B-SOiD (Hsu & Yttri 2021, Nat. Commun. 12:5188) and adds: multi-scale movement features (100 ms and 200 ms windows) and body-size-independent geometry; automatic selection of the clustering settings, with split and merge refinement of the clusters; stability checks across random seeds; hidden Markov model (HMM) smoothing of the labels over time; interactive annotation and optional guided labelling with your own labels; group statistics, a Group Predictor with permutation testing, and paradigm-specific reports. What CUBE does not require: manual behaviour labels, predefined behaviour categories, or frame-by-frame annotation. You can add labels later (see Guided labelling ) when you want clusters to follow behaviours you define. What you provide: video recordings of your animals. CUBE can run the DLC SuperAnimal quadruped model for you, or you can bring your own DLC output files (H5 or CSV). How CUBE relates to other tools # CUBE builds on B-SOiD and sits alongside other well-validated tools such as VAME and keypoint-MoSeq. These tools were designed for different needs, and none is best in every setting. The points below describe where CUBE's design differs. They reflect design choices rather than measured differences in performance. CUBE is under active development, and suggestions are very welcome. Where CUBE's design differs A single application from recording to figures. Video alignment, pose estimation, pre-processing, clustering, annotation and statistics are run from one point-and-click interface, so a complete analysis does not require programming or moving files between separate programs. Every stage of a run is saved to one folder. Temporally aware, animal-centred clustering with a reproducibility check. Features describe posture and movement in animal-centred (egocentric) coordinates together with the order of movements. Clustering is repeated across random seeds and the agreement between runs is reported. When agreement is low, CUBE builds a representative (medoid) or consensus partition, so that the result depends less on a single seed. Researcher-guided refinement and correction. Clusters are named by watching example clips, and can be merged, split or recombined by hand, with a dendrogram view to support the decision. Optional guided labelling lets you supply your own labelled examples, so manual input remains possible at each stage rather than only at the end. Built-in analysis and figures. The analyser produces ethograms, bout statistics, bar charts, transition analyses and group comparisons that highlight clusters whose usage changes between conditions, including behaviours that were not defined in adva

This page takes you from a folder of videos to named behaviours and your first figures. Each step links to the full guide, so you can read more only when you need to. Before you start CUBE is installed and launches (see Installation and launching ). Your videos are in one folder ( .mp4 , .avi or .mov ). Use the same camera position for animals you want to compare. For pose tracking you need a GPU. If you already have DeepLabCut output files (H5 or CSV), you can skip Step 1. The CUBE main window. Add video folders on the left, then run the step cards on the right from left to right. The ten steps Launch CUBE Double-click the CUBE icon on your Desktop (or Launch CUBE.bat ). The five step cards run left to right: DLC, pre-processing, clustering, annotation and analysis. Add your video folders Click Add under Video source folders and choose the folder with your videos. CUBE chooses an output folder for you automatically; use Change only if you want it somewhere else. Optional: group your animals If you will compare groups in Step 5, select a folder, type a group name and click Apply . You can also do this later in the analyser. Check the settings The defaults suit most datasets. Open DLC & Prep Settings only to set the recording frame rate or the minimum confidence for body points. The Bout Duration Filter (default 0.30 to 10 s) removes very brief or very long bouts before clustering. Step 1: track body points Click Step 1a for ordinary single-camera video, or Step 1b for a calibrated multi-camera rig. CUBE runs DeepLabCut and writes one filtered keypoint file per video. More on Step 1 . Step 2: pre-process Click Step 2 . CUBE checks the tracking quality and keeps the well-tracked body points. More on Step 2 . Step 3: discover behaviours Click Step 3 . CUBE extracts features, embeds them with UMAP, finds clusters with HDBSCAN, trains a classifier and smooths with a hidden Markov model. This takes tens of minutes for a typical dataset, and longer for large ones. More on Step 3 . Step 4: name the clusters Click Step 4 . Watch the example clips for each cluster and give it a name. Use the keys 1 to 9 to assign a behaviour, I to ignore a cluster and Ctrl + S to save. More on Step 4 . Step 5: analyse Click Step 5 to open the analyser on your output folder: ethograms, behaviour statistics, transitions and group comparisons. More on Step 5 . Export your figures Save figures and tables from the analyser. By default they go into the CUBE 5 - Final Data folder of your run. All results of one run live in a single timestamped CUBE results folder, so nothing is scattered. CUBE autosaves your session after every step. If you close it, click Load and choose the session file to continue where you stopped (see Autosave and loading ). If something goes wrong No clusters found, or odd results: see Troubleshooting . Step 1 fails or says pose tracking is not set up: choose Help → System check . If DeepLabCut or PyTorch is missing, double-click install_cube.bat again; it repairs the installation. The analyser shows no animals: choose the output folder that contains bout_lengths/ . Still stuck? Open an issue on GitHub with the log from the Pipeline Log panel.

Requirements # Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), an internet connection for the installation, and about 15 GB of free disk space. Nothing else. You do not need to install Python or Anaconda; the installer sets up its own. An NVIDIA graphics card is strongly recommended for DLC pose tracking (Step 1). It is not needed for Steps 2 to 5. Install (three steps) # Get CUBE. Download the ZIP from GitHub, right-click it and choose Extract All… , and put the folder somewhere simple, for example a folder called CUBE directly on your C: drive. Double-click install_cube.bat . It installs Python 3.12 in its own CUBE environment and every package CUBE needs: the analysis tools (Steps 2 to 5), DeepLabCut with PyTorch (Step 1) and Anipose (Step 1b). It picks the GPU or the CPU version of PyTorch automatically. The first run downloads several GB and takes 10 to 30 minutes. Wait for CUBE is installed . Running it again repairs a damaged installation. Start CUBE with the Desktop icon, or Launch CUBE.bat . The installer needs no administrator rights and changes nothing outside your Windows user profile and the CUBE folder. It writes install_log.txt ; send that file if you need help. Check the installation # In CUBE, choose Help → System check (or press the System check button). The report shows, for each step, what is installed and what is missing, whether your GPU was found, and how to fix problems. Copy report puts the text on the clipboard so you can paste it into an email. Without opening CUBE: python cube.py --check . Installing by hand (advanced) # CUBE is developed with Python 3.12.13 . From the CUBE folder, with any conda: conda env create -f environment.yml conda activate CUBE python -m pip install --no-deps -r requirements-lock.txt --no-deps is needed because DeepLabCut's metadata asks for numpy<2 while CUBE runs numpy 2.4; the lock file lists every package at its tested version. Use environment-cpu.yml and requirements-lock-cpu.txt on a computer without an NVIDIA GPU. Installer options (run from a terminal): install_cube.bat -Cpu , -Gpu , -Recreate . Important: DeepLabCut must be in the CUBE environment, not a separate one. Step 1 explains this and stops with a clear message if DeepLabCut or PyTorch is missing. Steps 2 to 5 do not need them. Which step do I need? # Your data Start at Single-camera videos, no pose files yet Step 1a Several synchronised cameras with a calibration recording Step 0 (if recorded with Bonsai or Doric), then Step 1b You already have DeepLabCut H5 or CSV files Step 2 You already ran Step 3 and want to name clusters Step 4 You already have named clusters and want statistics Step 5 Launching CUBE # Double-click the CUBE icon on the Desktop, or Launch CUBE.bat in the CUBE folder. The launcher finds the CUBE environment by itself; if it cannot, it tells you to run install_cube.bat . If CUBE closes with an error, a message box names the file CUBE_logs\last_launch_errors.txt ; Launch CUBE (console).bat keeps a window open so the error can be read. The CUBE main window. The five steps run left to right across the cards; progress and messages appear in the pipeline log. Two steps also run as standalone tools: Launch Analyser.bat (Behaviour Analyser, Step 5 only) and Launch Video Explorer.bat (Cluster Annotator, Step 4 only). From a terminal, with the CUBE environment active: python cube.py , python cube_analyser.py , python cube_video_explorer.py . The Theme button in the main window switches between the light and dark theme.

The window shows two alternative cards: Step 1a (2D DLC Inference) for ordinary single-camera video, and Step 1b (3D DLC + Anipose) for synchronised, calibrated multi-camera rigs. Run only one of them. Both feed into Step 2. If you already have DeepLabCut output files (H5 or CSV), skip to Step 2. Advanced DLC parameters: model type, SuperAnimal settings and detection thresholds. Settings that matter most (in DLC & Prep Settings ) Setting Default What it does Resolution Long edge 1280 (720p) Videos are resized before tracking Video adapt On Fine-tunes the model on your videos for better tracking Smart Adapt On Adapts the model once on a representative video and reuses it for all similar videos Adapt epochs 30 Training length for adaptation Pseudo threshold 0.40 Strictness of the automatic labels used for adaptation Post-filter Median (spike removal) Smoothing applied to the keypoint trajectories Filtered video On Writes an overlay video from the filtered keypoints Delete original Off Deletes the source video after processing. This cannot be undone Run CUBE prep On Runs Step 2 straight after tracking Recording FPS 30 Frames per second of your videos Advanced DLC Parameters holds the model choice (SuperAnimal Zoo model, recommended, or your own DLC project), the pose and detector architecture, confidence thresholds (pose confidence 0.3, bounding-box threshold 0.6), batch sizes and the keypoint overlay. What CUBE writes: one *_filtered.h5 file per video. The filter only removes jitter from keypoints DLC is already confident about; it does not fill gaps. Frames below the pose confidence keep their original values. Gap filling happens in Step 2/3. File matching: CUBE matches keypoint files to videos by file name, name prefix or a YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS time stamp. A file that cannot be matched is still analysed, but without video-linked features such as example clips. Uncalibrated rigs of up to three cameras: if no calibration exists and the rig has three or fewer cameras, Step 1b can fall back to a floor-plane homography fusion of the per-camera 2D keypoints (the homography fallback option in the 3D settings, on by default). The first time a camera pair is seen, a Homography Calibrator window opens: click four or more matching physical reference points in both camera views (for example the arena floor corners plus one wall point), then save. The result is cached and reused for every later session on that rig. This improves 2D coverage but does not claim 3D metric accuracy; a calibrated rig always triangulates in full 3D. See Section 12 .

What happens # Each keypoint file is converted to a standard format, so output from different DLC versions works. CUBE decides which body points to keep. A body point is kept when its confidence is high enough in at least 85% of sessions (defaults: minimum confidence 0.30, metric median , at least 6 body points kept). The result is written to bodypart_confidence_report.csv . When Step 3 loads the data, frames with low likelihood (below 0.30) are filled in from their neighbours, but only across gaps of up to 0.5 s. Longer dropouts are held at the last good value instead of being bridged by a straight line. A short moving average (70 ms) reduces single-frame jitter without shifting the timing. The settings are in DLC & Prep Settings (body-point selection) and Advanced CUBE Analysis Parameters → Feature extraction (likelihood threshold, boxcar smoothing).

How it works # Features. For each 100 ms bin CUBE computes distances between all tracked body points, their velocity and acceleration, and the variation within the bin, at 100 ms and 200 ms scales (plus a 50 ms scale for recordings of 60 frames per second or more). Egocentric (animal-centred) coordinates, left/right-symmetric features and, for side views, floor-referenced posture features are added. Features that describe the order of movements ("temporally-aware" features) are on by default. UMAP reduces these features to three dimensions. The neighbourhood size adapts to the recording length. HDBSCAN finds dense groups in the embedding. CUBE sweeps the minimum cluster size and picks the candidate whose clusters best survive a check against real behaviour bouts, within a preferred range of 15 to 25 clusters. Refinement. Clusters that are too mixed are split, and clusters that are barely distinguishable from a sibling are merged. Rare clusters (below 0.2% of the time) are removed. Classifier. A random forest is trained on the labelled bins and then labels every bin of every video, including sessions that were not used for clustering. HMM smoothing removes flicker between labels (see Section 7 ). Bout building. Runs of the same label become bouts. Short interruptions of up to 0.3 s are bridged, and bouts outside 0.3 to 10 s are filtered out (the Bout Duration Filter in the main window). Things you may want to adjust # Body-region weights (optional). In Advanced CUBE Analysis Parameters , the button Body-Region Weights (optional)... lets you give more or less weight to a body region (Head/Mouth, Forelimbs, Hindlimbs, Trunk/Back, Neck, Tail; other body points go into "Other"). Each region has a slider from 0.1 to 3.0; 1.0 means no change, and leaving every slider at 1.0 applies no weighting. A typical use: if a subtle mouth behaviour such as licking is mixed with other behaviours in one cluster, try a Head/Mouth weight of 2 to 2.5 and rerun Step 3. The last weights you apply are remembered across projects. The Advanced CUBE Analysis Parameters window, where the feature, UMAP, HDBSCAN, classifier and HMM settings live. UMAP embeddings of open field recordings, coloured by cluster. Example from the public data of Sturman et al. (2020). Automatic down-weighting of poorly tracked body points (on). A body point that is poorly tracked in many sessions is given a lower weight automatically. Weights you set yourself always take precedence. Turned-away frames (on). When the animal turns away from the camera, face tracking becomes unreliable. CUBE flags a 100 ms bin as turned away when a majority (threshold 0.5) of the seven face points have low confidence for that session. Flagged windows shorter than 1 s are ignored, and windows less than 0.5 s apart are merged. Flagged bins are excluded from clustering and written under one extra cluster id, Turned Away (one number above your highest real cluster). Labelled videos show a "TURNED AWAY" banner on flagged frames. Untick Exclude turned-away frames from clustering to switch the exclusion off. When reading statistics, keep in mind that a behaviour interrupted by a turned-away window appears as two shorter bouts, and that percentages of session time include the turned-away time, so groups that turn away at different rates can differ for that reason alone. Low-confidence clusters. After clustering, cluster_confidence.csv flags clusters that mainly reflect low tracking confidence, so you can check them before spending time on annotation. The option Auto-flag impure clusters is off by default because it can wrongly flag real behaviours; always check example clips before trusting a flag. Cluster count. Leave Target cluster count at 0 for automatic selection within the preferred range, or set a number to steer Step 3 towards it. See Section 8 . Stability checks. By default CUBE repeats the embedding and clustering with 6 random seeds and reports how similar the results are ( cluster_stability.png ). If the agreement is low (mean ARI below 0.55), CUBE automatically builds a more robust partition: by default it uses the most representative seed (medoid) and escalates to consensus clustering only if that seed is not trustworthy. These steps add runtime. You can switch them off or change them in the Advanced window. Plots written by Step 3 # File What it shows umap_embedding.png , umap_3d.html The embedding coloured by cluster (the HTML file is interactive) cluster_validity.png Per-cluster silhouette and the HDBSCAN condensed tree. Use it to spot weak clusters before annotation split_merge_refinement.png Before and after view of the refinement (only written when it changed the labels) cluster_hierarchy_postures.png A dendrogram of the clusters with a typical posture under each one cluster_trajectories_aligned.png , cluster_trajectories_unaligned.png The average movement of each cluster, with and without a common heading cluster_stability.png Agreement between random seeds transition_matrix.png , hmm_transition_matrix.png , hmm_syntax_network.png How behaviours follow each other state_space_projection.png How the behavioural states sit in a shared low-dimensional space

x: Launch: click Step 4 (the Video Annotation card), or run cube_video_explorer.py . Cluster hierarchy with a typical posture for each cluster (elevated plus maze example), which helps you decide what to name each cluster. Workflow # Open the Step 3 output folder. The explorer loads the example clips of each cluster. For each cluster, play several clips and assign a behaviour name (for example "Rearing", "Grooming", "Locomotion"). Use Previous and Next (or the arrow keys) to move between clusters. You can give several clusters the same name when they show the same behaviour at different speeds or body angles; they are then analysed together as one behaviour. Save the session. Your names appear in the Analyser. Clusters you did not name are shown as "Cluster N". Keyboard shortcuts: arrow keys move between clusters, Space replays the clip, N creates a new behaviour group, I ignores the current cluster, 1 to 9 assign the cluster to behaviour group 1 to 9, Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z undoes the last assignment. Tips # Watch several clips per cluster before naming it; behaviour within a cluster can vary. The reserved Turned Away cluster has example clips like any other. It appears as an unnamed "Cluster N" (N is your highest real cluster id plus one). A glance at a clip confirms it is footage of the animal turned away; naming it "Turned Away" keeps it labelled consistently. The Video Explorer has a second tab, Guided labelling , for when you want clusters to follow behaviours you define yourself (see Guided labelling ).

Launch: click Step 5 (the Behaviour Analysis card), or run cube_analyser.py . Section 6 describes every tab. An ethogram: human labels, CUBE with labels (held-out video) and blind clusters over one minute (open field example). Reading the Turned Away cluster. When turned-away exclusion was on (the default), one extra cluster id represents time the animal was judged to be turned away from the camera. It is a tracking artefact, not a behaviour, so leave it out of behavioural interpretation, as you would an unnamed cluster. Two effects are worth knowing: a behaviour bout interrupted by a turned-away window is split into two shorter bouts (more bouts, shorter mean duration), and "% time" values are computed over the whole session including turned-away time. The transition-matrix plots do not show Turned Away as a state. Behaviour sequences as a Sankey diagram: bar height is state occupancy, ribbon width is transition flow.

You will find: one folder per run, with everything from Steps 0 to 5 inside it. State-space projection written to the plots folder (open field example). Every run writes into a single timestamped folder, CUBE results <date>_<time> , which CUBE creates inside the folder you processed (or inside the global output folder, if you set one): CUBE results <date>_<time>/ CUBE 0 - Corrected 3D vids/ (Step 0, multi-camera recordings only) CUBE 1a - 2D DLC/ (Step 1a: tracking output per video) CUBE 1b - 3D DLC/<session>/ (Step 1b: 3D output per session) CUBE 2 - Preclustering files/ (Step 2: cleaned keypoint files per folder) CUBE 3 - Clusters/ (Step 3: everything described below) CUBE 5 - Final Data/ (Step 5: exported comparison figures) Older results that use the previous folder layout are still found automatically. The Analyser loads the _hmm files when they exist and falls back to the raw files otherwise. To analyse the raw classifier labels, rename or delete the _hmm files. Frame label files. In *_frame_labels[_hmm].csv , the label column is the final label (after Turned Away marking and bout bridging), and raw_label is the unmodified prediction for that frame.

Open it with the Step 5 card ( Behaviour Analysis ), or run cube_analyser.py . The analyser opens on the Live Preview tab. Open a CUBE output folder to begin; the other tabs hold full analyses, metric tables, unbiased analytics, the behaviour explorer, the Group Predictor and paradigm results. The left panel holds the folder controls: Open: Folder loads a Step 3 output folder, Load Mapping loads a saved mapping from clusters to behaviour names, File and FPS select one animal, Group Editor merges clusters into named behaviour groups, Analyse & Preview draws the analysis for the selected file, and Save Results and Save All Results export figures and tables. On opening a folder, the Analyser finds all *_bout_lengths_hmm.csv files (or the raw ones) in the bout_lengths folder, loads one animal per file, and loads your Step 4 names automatically. The tabs are: Tab What it is for Live Preview An ethogram of the selected file that updates as you edit behaviour groups Full Analysis The plots for the selected file, drawn by Analyse & Preview Metrics Table The per-behaviour metrics of the selected file Combined Analysis All animals together: set groups, compare them, export Unbiased Analytics Statistics, effect sizes and automatic reclustering across groups Behavioral Explorer How transitions, dwell times and sequences differ between groups Group Predictor Whether the behavioural profile can tell groups apart Paradigm Results Paradigm-specific reports (needs arena tracing) Combined Analysis tab # The tab shows the animal list on the left and the analysis on the right. Labels. Give every animal a Label 1 (usually its experimental group, for example "Control" or "Drug"), and optionally Label 2 and Label 3 / Animal ID . Group by chooses which label defines the groups. Label 3 is also used to pair the same animal across time points. Run Combined Analysis draws a behavioural fingerprint heatmap (how much of its time each animal spends in each cluster), ethograms (a timeline per animal with coloured bars), and group comparisons. Export Combined saves them. Min bout dur (s) (default 0.3) drops bouts shorter than this from every loaded animal before any statistic is computed, matching the pipeline's own floor. Changing it re-filters the loaded animals immediately, and the value is remembered per source folder. Set it to 0 to see the unfiltered bouts. Unbiased Analytics tab # Experimental design (under Statistical Settings , above Group by ): Independent groups (default): different animals in each group, for example Control, Treatment A and Treatment B. The overall test is Kruskal-Wallis and the pairwise follow-up is Dunn's test (Mann-Whitney U if scikit-posthocs is not installed). P-values are corrected for the false discovery rate across every cluster and panel shown together, so a star means the same thing on every panel. Repeated measures : the same animals measured at several levels of Group by (for example Baseline, Day 3, Day 7). Give matching animals the same Label 3 / Animal ID at every level. Only animals present at every level are used, and at least 3 matched animals are required. The overall test is a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (2 levels) or Friedman's test (3 or more levels), with pairwise Wilcoxon follow-ups and the same false discovery rate correction. The status bar reports how many animals were matched and how many were excluded. A mixed design (independent groups, each followed over time) is not available. What the statistics report for each cluster (independent groups): whether the cluster is present in each group at all (a prevalence test, because a cluster that is absent in one group is a different kind of effect from a difference in amount), then, among animals that show it, whether its frequency or duration differs between groups. The result table is exported with the figures. Plot modes Mode What it shows Top-N Bar The N most frequent clusters ranked by group mean Volcano Effect size against significance for all clusters Heatmap Cluster by animal usage matrix, ordered by Ward clustering Elbow/Silhouette Fit quality for different numbers of merged groups Cluster Hierarchy A live view of the cluster dendrogram (see Recombination guide ) Guided Merge Automatic merging that stops by itself (see Recombination guide ) Recombination A dendrogram of clusters grouped by how their usage changes (see Recombination guide ) Dist Matrix Pairwise behavioural distance between animals Transitions Cluster-to-cluster transition probabilities Grp Transitions Group comparison of transitions, pair by pair (Welch's t-test, volcano plot) Cluster Stats Per-cluster summary: mean bout length, frequency, total time Cluster Validity Silhouette diagram and UMAP scatter of the primary clustering. The condensed-tree view is in plots/cluster_validity.png The Metric selector in the bar, volcano and heatmap views also offers each cluster's movement signature from cluster_kinematics.csv . Behavioral Explorer tab # Group-level views of sequence structure: Diff Heatmap (difference between transition matrices of two groups), Dwell Violin (distribution of dwell times for each state and group), Sankey (flow of behavioural sequences per group), Group Transitions (transition probabilities per group) Group Networks (circular transition networks per group, above-chance edges only) and Energy Landscape (an occupancy-based landscape over the UMAP embedding: common states are valleys and rare states are peaks). Group Predictor Tab # The Group Predictor asks whether the full behavioural profile of an animal can tell its experimental group. It runs three models (based on frequency, total duration and transition probability), each evaluated with leave-one-out cross-validation and a permutation test. Assign experimental groups in the Combined Analysis tab first. Click Run Models with the default settings. Check the permutation p-value (green means significant) and click View on the best model to see its confusion matrix and the feature
h: Detecting one group among several (target group, contrasts and group statistics)

x: What it is for: HDBSCAN often splits one real behaviour into two or three clusters because of small pose differences. Recombination takes the N raw clusters down to a smaller set that matches distinguishable behaviours. The Unbiased Analytics tab offers three ways to do this. They answer different questions. The three methods # Method View What decides a merge Stops at Best for Manual k-sweep Recombination You pick the number of groups, k Exactly k groups Seeing what forcing 3, 5 or 8 groups looks like, side by side Recombination with pose-distance cap Recombination The same, but a proposed group is rejected (split back into its raw clusters) if any pair inside it is too far apart in pose space k groups, minus any rejected merges Checking that a chosen k merges clusters that look alike, not just clusters whose usage changes together Guided Merge Guided Merge The algorithm merges the closest pair by usage pattern, but only if the pair is also close in pose space and clearly better than the next-best rejected option Automatically, when no further merge is justified Not having to choose k, and having a reproducible, defensible starting point for merging All three start from the same distance between clusters: 70% correlation of each cluster's usage pattern across your experimental groups plus 30% cosine similarity of the clusters' outgoing transition profiles. What differs is whether a second, independent signal, pose similarity, can veto a merge. Why a pose-distance cap exists # The blended distance only looks at how a cluster's usage changes between groups and how it transitions to other clusters. Two clusters can match on both for reasons unrelated to being the same behaviour, such as a shared arousal state or a coincidence in a small dataset. The pose-distance cap adds an independent check: it measures how different the clusters' movement and posture really are, using the same features UMAP and HDBSCAN were trained on, and only lets a merge through when the clusters are close on both criteria. Requirement. The cap, Guided Merge and the Cluster Hierarchy view need model/cluster_feature_centroids.npz , which Step 3 saves automatically. Runs from before this file existed do not have it; rerun Step 3 to create it (Steps 4 and 5 do not need to be redone). Until then the cap control is greyed out and the views explain why. Backfill pose data (approximate). A faster alternative for old runs: it builds pseudo-centroids from the saved embedding instead of true feature-space centroids, so it needs no raw keypoint files and runs instantly. It is a lower-fidelity approximation, because distances between clusters in a UMAP embedding are only locally meaningful. Everything built from it is marked APPROXIMATE , and the button never overwrites a real cluster_feature_centroids.npz . Use it for a quick look and rerun Step 3 for results you will publish. Parameters # Parameter Where Default What it does What changing it means k to save / compare k values Recombination 5 / 3,5,8 How many merged groups the manual sweep makes Lower k lumps more and is easier to read but may merge distinct behaviours; higher k stays closer to the raw clustering Pose-distance cap (percentile) Recombination 100 (off) Only clusters within this percentile of the closest pose distances may merge Lower is stricter. Values under about 10 can reject almost everything, which suggests k should be lower before you merge Guided Merge cap % Guided Merge 50 (median) The ceiling of pose distance Guided Merge may consider at all Lower is more conservative. Values well above 50 to 60 remove the pose constraint Guided Merge min gap Guided Merge 0.15 The best remaining merge must be at least this much closer (as a fraction of its own distance) than the closest pair that pose distance already ruled out Lower accepts more borderline merges (fewer, larger groups); higher stops earlier Save source Save Reclustered Groups Manual (k-sweep) Whether Save as Preset and Push to Group Editor export the k-sweep groups or the Guided Merge groups Defaults to the view you are looking at Reading the outputs # Recombination title. When the cap is active it reports how many proposed merges were rejected at each k (for example "2 of 5 proposed merges rejected"). If many are rejected, your k probably lumps clusters that do not look alike: try a lower k, or keep the smaller groups. Guided Merge labels. Each merged group ( RG-1 , RG-2 , ...) is labelled with the raw cluster ids inside it. Guided Merge table. One row per accepted merge, with the pair, their blended distance, pose distance and percentile, usage correlation and transition similarity. A merge with a high pose-distance percentile and only a moderate correlation deserves a second look before you rely on it. Cophenetic correlation (bottom of the table) is a number between -1 and 1 that says how faithfully the dendrogram represents the distances. Below roughly 0.7 to 0.8, be sceptical of any cut of the tree. Which method to use # A quick summary plot: manual k-sweep with the cap off. Pick a k that gives a readable number of groups (5 to 8 is usually legible). A write-up that has to justify the merges: Guided Merge with the defaults, and cite the table's pose-distance percentile and correlation for each merge. Someone doubts a merge you made by hand: open Recombination at your k, set a strict cap (20 to 30) and see whether the merge survives. Compare with the Cluster Hierarchy view: clusters on clearly distant branches are a real reason to reconsider. Guided Merge merges nothing, or everything into two groups: if nothing merges, raise the cap % first, then lower the min gap. If it merges too much, lower the cap % first, then raise the min gap. Controls are greyed out: the run predates cluster_feature_centroids.npz ; rerun Step 3.

This tab reports paradigm-specific measures. It has content only for sessions that were run with environmental context tracing switched on (see Behavioural paradigms and arena context ) and that have a session_env_context.json file. Sessions without it show a message instead of a plot. Load sessions in the Combined Analysis tab as usual (a mix with and without arena data is fine). Open the Paradigm Results tab and click Refresh from Loaded Sessions . The sub-view that matches your traced paradigm is selected for you; use the Paradigm Sub-view list to browse the others. Sub-view Paradigm What it shows Generic Any (default for custom and open field) Whole-arena occupancy heatmap and region-time bar. For the open field also total distance, centre-zone entries (looks for a traced region with "center" in its name), the centre-zone time course and the distribution of mean speed Y-Maze Alternation y_maze Per-arm occupancy, spontaneous alternation %, total arm entries and an arm-entry sequence strip Elevated Plus Maze elevated_plus_maze Open- and closed-arm occupancy, % open-arm time and entries, latency to the first open-arm entry, total arm entries, an open-arm time course, and a head-dip proxy (nose crossing the traced edge; a geometric proxy, not a validated classifier) Discrimination Index novel_object Investigation density around each object, discrimination index (tested against chance), total exploration time, nose-to-novel-object distance, investigation bout durations and latency to first contact Sociability / Social Novelty three_chamber Per-chamber occupancy, the Phase 1 sociability index and the Phase 2 social-novelty index (each tested against 0), chamber entries, nose-to-stranger distance, investigation bouts and latency Place Preference / CPP place_preference Pre/post occupancy, preference index (tested against 0), a cumulative chamber-crossing time course and, with Repeated measures and a real pre-test phase, a paired pre/post comparison Fear Conditioning (Contextual) fear_conditioning_contextual Freezing % time course (mean ± SEM, shock shading in Acquisition only), behaviour-proportion time course, extinction curve, cross-phase fear trajectory and an ethogram with shock markers. A locomotor control (path length outside freezing bouts) is always shown Fear Conditioning (Cued) fear_conditioning_cued Everything in the contextual view, plus tone shading on every phase with tone trials, latency to freeze after the tone, and a paired pre-tone versus during-tone comparison (within-animal Wilcoxon test) Approach/Avoid Events Any Trajectories with each detected event drawn as an arrow (green = approach, red = avoid), the event rate and target distribution. This is a rule-based heuristic that has not been validated against expert scoring, so treat it as a starting point for review Fear conditioning needs no arena tracing, because freezing is the readout. You enter a one-time protocol schedule (baseline, trials, shock and tone timing for each phase) in the Protocol Schedule tab of the Environments window. The phase is read from Label 2 (for example Acquisition, Extinction, Recall), the context from Label 1 and the animal from Label 3 . Freezing comes from a behaviour you named "Freezing" in Step 4 (the preferred source); if there is none, CUBE falls back to a multi-body-point immobility detector that is marked "(auto-detected)" wherever it appears and has not been validated against hand-scored freezing. Shock and tone shading come from the configured schedule, so they will not align if the real timing of your rig differs. Every sub-view also shows grouped bar charts of the % time each cluster, and each group, spends in each traced region. Bar charts show each animal's own value as an open ring on top of its group's bar. Statistics. Between-group comparisons use the same Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn tests, with false discovery rate correction, as Unbiased Analytics. Discrimination Index and CPP also get a one-sample test against a fixed reference (chance or zero), marked with daggers so it is never confused with the stars used for between-group brackets. Occupancy heatmaps show real position density. The region and object outlines on top are an approximation (the convex hull of the positions recorded in or near each shape), not the exact traced boundary, and are labelled "(approx.)". Save All Results (Combined Analysis tab) includes the figures of every applicable sub-view and a paradigm_derived_metrics.csv summary. For the requirements and limits of each paradigm, see Behavioral_Paradigms_Reference.md . Environmental Context & Object Interaction (opt-in) # Switch it on in the Environments, Objects, Paradigms... window; this also enables Configure Arena, Regions & Objects... , which opens the tracing window. The Environments, Objects and Paradigms window: opt-in environmental context, kinematic directedness and region-aware cluster splitting. Paradigm. You first choose one paradigm for the project: Open Field, Novel Object / Animal Recognition, Y-Maze, Elevated Plus Maze, Three-Chamber Test, Place Preference / CPP, Fear Conditioning (Contextual or Cued), or Custom. It decides which drawing tools, name suggestions and role lists you see (fear conditioning needs a protocol schedule instead of traced regions). A batch that mixes experiment types needs separate CUBE projects. Tab 1, Define Reference Arena. Trace the arena boundary and any named regions or objects on a reference frame by clicking points and then Finish Shape . Every shape, including the boundary, needs at least 3 points. Shapes that matter for the paradigm's measures get a Role (for example Familiar or Novel for Novel Object objects, Arm or Hub for Y-Maze regions). The measure uses the role, not the display name, so you can name shapes as you like. A warning appears when a paradigm's measure cannot yet be computed (for example Y-Maze needs at least 3 regions with the role Arm). Save as Template... and Load Template... store the parad

What it is for: CUBE's clusters sometimes do not isolate a behaviour you know well (rare behaviours, or behaviours seen only when the animal turns away). Guided labelling lets you mark examples of your behaviours so the clustering follows them. Nothing changes until you label; a run without labels is identical to a blind run. Blind CUBE clusters (left), CUBE with guided labels on held-out videos (middle) and the human labels on the same embedding (right). Open field, public data of Sturman et al. (2020). Guided labelling is the second tab of the Video Explorer (Step 4). Steps # Finish Step 3 on your data. Open Step 4 and choose the Guided labelling tab (it also opens from any folder inside a run; use "Open a CUBE run" if none is found). Add your behaviours (a name and a colour each). Two names are reserved: Background ("none of my behaviours") and Neither . Label in either of two ways: (a) play a video, press Start and End , then click the coloured behaviour button (or keys 1 to 9); click a segment and another button to change it later; (b) answer question cards , with one coloured button per behaviour plus Neither, Skip and Stop. Ask about focuses the questions on one behaviour, which helps for a rare one. When you have marked every instance of your behaviours in a video, tick This video is fully labelled . The unmarked time then counts as true negatives. This is the only way to measure false positives honestly. After each round of questions, the tool reports leakage on your fully labelled videos and says STOP? when it has stopped improving (less than 2 points over 2 rounds). Then label a different animal fully, or add examples of what is not your behaviour. Save results writes your labels, the guided behaviour track and an Analyser-ready folder, CUBE 3b - Guided behaviours (bout lengths, cluster_behaviour_mapping.tsv and behaviour_groups.json ; several clusters of one behaviour are saved as one behaviour group). Produce plots writes plots/guided/ (before and after UMAPs, Coverage, Leakage and Ratio before and after, the labelled hierarchy and tables). Closing the annotator asks you to save if labels changed. Rerunning Step 3 applies the labels to the clustering: poorly tracked bins are reclustered separately, your bout lengths and transitions feed the HMM, and your names appear on the hierarchy and trajectory plots. What to expect. Example results on the public open field and elevated plus maze data, with whole videos held out (Coverage % / Leakage %): elevated plus maze Grooming 99 / 6 and Head Dip 96 / 23, against 50 / 10 and 2 / 59 for CUBE's blind clusters; open field Supported 94 / 15, Unsupported 74 / 17 and Grooming 70 / 8, against 12 / 25, 0 and 0. Behaviours with only a few dozen labelled bins (for example elevated plus maze Unprotected Stretch and open field Jumping) are not learned. After about 7 minutes of simulated labelling (400 clips), elevated plus maze Rearing reached 53 / 20 and Protected Stretch 75 / 38. The before/after plot in the tool is in-sample (a check of how well the clusters now match your labels); held-out accuracy needs labelled videos that were not used for training. The same comparison on the elevated plus maze. Tips and pitfalls # Label several behaviours in the same videos . Behaviours labelled in different videos teach the classifier to recognise the animal instead (the tab warns you). Do not rely on the "Neither" answer as a trained class until you have many examples spread over several videos; it is used to check false positives. Behaviours that occur together (for example Guarding then Licking) are exported both separately and as a combined "family". If your reference labels come from another tool, check their time base. The elevated plus maze and open field example videos are 25 fps, but CUBE bins assume 30 fps (one bin is 0.12 s of label time). Close and reopen the annotator after updating CUBE; an old window can drop newer label-file keys when it saves. Settings ( guided_* ), file layout, method and validation are described in GUIDED_LABELLING_REFERENCE.md .

How it works # An HMM is fitted to the classifier output, estimating how likely each behaviour is to persist and to switch to each other behaviour (the transition matrix). Viterbi decoding then finds the single most probable label sequence. An ethogram around a head dip (elevated plus maze example): human labels, CUBE with labels and blind clusters. By default CUBE uses the version that works with the classifier's probabilities instead of hard labels, so an uncertain bin is smoothed with less confidence than a certain one. It works at 100 ms bin resolution, and each cluster gets its own persistence prior derived from its mean bout duration, so naturally brief behaviours are not over-smoothed. These are the defaults ( hmm_emission_mode soft, hmm_smoothing_level bin, hmm_transition_prior per_cluster). Setting them to categorical , frame and global restores the earlier hard-label, frame-level behaviour with one flat persistence prior. Two sets of outputs # Every output is written in a raw version and an HMM-smoothed version ( *_frame_labels.csv and *_frame_labels_hmm.csv , *_bout_lengths.csv and *_bout_lengths_hmm.csv ). The Analyser uses the HMM files by default; rename or delete them to use the raw labels. Two transition matrices # transition_matrix.png is empirical: it counts every consecutive pair of frames in the raw classifier output, with the diagonal masked. hmm_transition_matrix.png shows the matrix the HMM learned, in two panels: the matrix itself and a version with the diagonal removed and the rows renormalised, which shows the switching pattern independently of self-persistence.

Open it from: Advanced CUBE Analysis... in the main window. The window is organised in sections, and the defaults shown here are the values the app uses when you press Restore Defaults . The defaults are chosen to work for most datasets, so change a setting only for a specific reason. Settings for arena tracing and paradigms are in their own window, Environments, Objects, Paradigms... (see below). The Advanced CUBE Analysis Parameters window. Publication defaults are pre-set; change a setting only for a specific reason. Feature Extraction # Setting Default What it does Egocentric alignment (2D and 3D) On Adds animal-centred body-point coordinates next to the standard geometry features. It helps posture-defined behaviours (for example reared versus supported) and can dilute an already well-separated one (for example grooming), so it is a trade-off Body normalisation Off Divides distances by the nose-to-tail-base length (needs both body points) PCA pre-reduction auto auto reduces the features when their number reaches one fifth of the number of samples; on always; off never PCA pre-UMAP (inner) auto A separate PCA step used by UMAP itself. Leave on auto unless you need both Long lag drift (2 to 3 s) Off Lagged features for sustained states such as freezing or guarding Long scale bins (500 ms and 1 s) Off Coarse time bins for slow, sustained behaviours Likelihood threshold 0.30 Frames below this DLC likelihood are filled in from their neighbours Boxcar smooth (s) 0.07 Length of the moving average applied to the trajectories Adaptive visibility features On Adds per-body-point confidence features so turned-away or occluded bins form their own cluster instead of polluting real behaviours Visibility adaptive percentile 10 Per-body-point confidence floor, on top of the likelihood threshold. Raise it to 15 to 20 if turned-away frames do not separate cleanly Visibility feature weight 2.0 How strongly the visibility signal shapes the embedding (1.0 means no extra weight) Face-to-limb proximity feature weight 2.0 How strongly nose or jaw to paw proximity shapes the embedding (1.0 means no extra weight) Isolated-limb feature weight 1.5 How strongly a single raised limb and its sustained hold shape the embedding (1.0 means no extra weight) Exclude turned-away frames from clustering On Excludes turned-away bins from training and labels them "Turned Away" Turned-away confidence threshold 0.5 The share of face points with low confidence that flags a bin as turned away. Raise it to make detection more conservative Auto-flag impure clusters Off Folds low-silhouette clusters into a separate "Low-Quality Cluster" label. Off by default because it can wrongly flag a real behaviour; check the example clips before trusting a flag Impure-cluster silhouette threshold 0 0 reuses the split silhouette threshold below (0.20) Body-Region Weights (optional)... Uniform Opens the panel described under Step 3 Two more turned-away settings have no control in the window and can be set in the saved session's engine configuration: the minimum window length ( turned_away_min_window_s , default 1.0 s) and the merge gap ( turned_away_merge_gap_s , default 0.5 s). UMAP Embedding # Setting Default What it does Full-data threshold 10,000 Below this number of bins all bins are used; larger recordings are subsampled Train fraction 0.75 The share of bins used to fit UMAP when subsampling Subsample strategy iid block uses contiguous blocks, which is better for short or rare behaviours (opt-in) Block length (bins, block mode) 17 Length of each block n_neighbors 0 (auto) 0 scales the neighbourhood with the recording length. The B-SOiD reference value is 60 n_components 3 Dimensions of the embedding min_dist 0.10 Point packing. Below 0.05 can destabilise the density graph used by HDBSCAN Random seed 42 For reproducibility HDBSCAN Clustering # Setting Default What it does Distance metric euclidean Also manhattan or cosine Cluster selection method leaf leaf gives finer clusters, eom larger ones, both tries both and keeps the better Cluster Count Guidance # Setting Default What it does Target cluster count 0 (auto) A number above 0 steers Step 3 towards that count Preferred range, low and high 15 and 25 In automatic mode CUBE prefers solutions inside this range. Ignored when a target is set Selection mode occurrence_persistence_ranged How the clustering candidate is chosen (see below) Overshoot penalty 0.01 Penalty per cluster above the high bound; used only by floor_soft_cap Cluster hierarchy plot On Saves the dendrogram that guides manual merging Hierarchy linkage method ward Also average or complete Min cluster frequency (%) 0.2 Clusters below this share of the total time are removed before the classifier is trained Selection modes. occurrence_persistence_ranged (default) ranks candidates by how well their clusters survive a test against real behaviour bouts, while respecting the preferred range (a hard floor at the low end, a soft penalty above the high end). occurrence_persistence uses the same ranking but ignores the range and can settle on very few clusters. floor_soft_cap ranks by DBCV or silhouette, avoids the low bound and lightly penalises overshoot. legacy is an earlier rule that can collapse to very few clusters. Iterative Split / Merge Refinement # After the first clustering, clusters that are mixed are split and clusters that are barely separated are merged, up to a few rounds. In order: Split. A cluster whose mean silhouette is below the split threshold is re-embedded and re-clustered locally. A split is accepted only if the local result is a stable sub-partition, so noise alone does not cause a split. Merge. Sibling clusters that separated at low persistence in the HDBSCAN condensed tree, and that are also close in the embedding, are merged. Prune. Rare clusters are removed. Steps 1 to 3 repeat up to the iteration limit and stop early when a round changes nothing. Every decision is written to the run log, and every accepted s

x: CUBE saves your session automatically after every completed step, to a file named autosave.pipeline_session.json in the Output folder shown at the top of the main window. The session holds your video folders, group labels, parameter settings, step-completion flags and the DLC model state. It does not hold the numerical data, which stays in the output files. To continue later: Start CUBE again. Click Load (top right) and choose the session file. Your folders and settings are restored, and the step cards show which steps are complete. Run the next step. Click Save to keep a named copy of the session at any time, for example one per experiment. Compatibility Mode # Version 2.1 corrected several defaults. To reproduce results from an earlier run exactly: Open Advanced CUBE Analysis. Under Reproducibility and Methodology , set Compatibility mode to legacy_v2 . This restores the earlier values of umap_min_dist (0.0 instead of 0.1), hdbscan_mcs_anchor ( full instead of embedding ) and angular_fallback (on instead of off). A setting you changed yourself is never overridden. The version of the defaults is stamped into feature_config.json and validation_report.json , so each output folder records which defaults were used.

Installation and start-up problems # Always begin with Help → System check (or python cube.py --check ). It names what is missing and the fix. Symptom Cause and fix Launching says CUBE has not been installed The CUBE environment is missing. Run install_cube.bat (it can be run any number of times). install_cube.bat stops with a network message A download was interrupted or blocked. Run it again; finished packages are not downloaded again. On a company network, ask IT to allow pypi.org , conda.anaconda.org , github.com and download.pytorch.org . The installer says requirements-lock.txt was not found CUBE was started from inside the ZIP. Right-click the ZIP, choose Extract All… , and run the installer from the extracted folder. Windows SmartScreen blocks the .bat file Choose More info → Run anyway . The scripts are plain text and can be read in Notepad. Pose tracking is not set up when starting Step 1 DeepLabCut or PyTorch is missing from the environment. Run install_cube.bat . If you already have DeepLabCut output, start at Step 2. System check: no GPU available Without an NVIDIA GPU this is expected: everything works and only Step 1 is slow. With a GPU, install the current driver from nvidia.com/drivers (version 580 or newer is required by the GPU build), restart, then run install_cube.bat -Gpu . System check: several OpenCV packages installed Run install_cube.bat to restore a single OpenCV. CUBE closes immediately or shows an error box Open CUBE_logs\last_launch_errors.txt , or double-click Launch CUBE (console).bat to read the message in a window. Send it together with the Copy report text from System check. Path too long errors Keep video folders short and close to the top of a drive, for example a folder called Mouse1 inside a folder called Videos. Disk fills up during a run Results and corrected videos are large. System check reports free space; choose an output drive with 50 GB or more. "No clusters found" after Step 3 # Read the log: HDBSCAN may have labelled every point as noise. Try a larger n_neighbors or a smaller minimum cluster size. Check the tracking quality: open a few keypoint files and confirm that likelihood values are mostly above 0.6. If too many frames are being interpolated (see the "% interpolated" line of the log), lower the likelihood threshold. Low classifier cross-validation accuracy # Check that Min cluster frequency is not too low; tiny clusters are hard to classify. Keep the class weight on balanced , which handles unequal cluster sizes. Look at umap_3d.html . If all points are in one clump, try a larger n_neighbors or a smaller min_dist . HMM smoothing gives implausibly long bouts # Open hmm_transition_matrix.png . The diagonal should be high (about 0.95 to 0.99) but not 1.0. Try fewer Baum-Welch iterations, which leave the matrix closer to its prior. Compare *_bout_lengths.csv and *_bout_lengths_hmm.csv . To analyse the raw labels, delete or rename the _hmm files. The number of clusters looks wrong # Read the split and merge lines of the run log. Every accepted split or merge is logged, so you can trace which clusters changed and why. A merge refused by the region-aware guard is logged as REFUSED: region-aware merge guard . Open plots/cluster_validity.png (or the Analyser's Cluster Validity mode) to see the values the decisions were based on, and model/split_merge_log.json for the fate of every split. If merging looks too aggressive, lower the merge threshold. If splitting creates tiny, low-confidence fragments, raise the split threshold or reduce the iterations. To switch refinement off, set the split threshold and the merge threshold to 0 and rerun. With region-aware splitting on, check the [region-split] lines of the log. Lower the impurity threshold or the minority floor if it looks too conservative, or raise them if it over-splits. The partition changes a lot between runs # Look at cluster_stability.png . A low agreement means the embedding itself is seed-sensitive for your data. CUBE then builds a more robust partition automatically (see Reproducibility and Methodology ); the log line [CONSENSUS-AUTO] says when it did so and why. DLC inference fails in Step 1 # Check the CUDA drivers if you use a GPU, and confirm that DLC works on its own outside CUBE. Try with Smart Adapt off. It can fail when the adaptation video does not contain enough varied frames. Check that OpenCV can read your video files: open one in a video player and try cv2.VideoCapture(path).isOpened() in Python. The Analyser shows no animals or empty tables # Confirm that the folder you chose contains a bout_lengths folder. Confirm that it holds *_bout_lengths_hmm.csv or *_bout_lengths.csv files. File names must end in _bout_lengths.csv or _bout_lengths_hmm.csv . Group Predictor shows near-chance accuracy for every model # Common causes: the groups really are behaviourally similar in this recording context; there are too few animals (fewer than 6 per group is very hard); the group assignments are wrong; or the wrong feature source is selected, in which case try Custom mode with a targeted set of clusters. See GROUP_PREDICTOR_REFERENCE.md for more. "invalid command name" messages when closing # These tkinter messages are harmless. A few scheduled screen updates run after their windows were closed. They do not affect results or saved files.

x: Overview # You need Step 0 output: corrected, synchronised videos from bonsai_video_corrector.py . A calibration recording: a Charuco board recorded by all cameras, run through the same Step 0 and with "calibration" in its session name. CUBE finds it and creates calibration.toml automatically. A calibration.toml made by hand still works as a backup (see Camera Calibration ). Software: aniposelib , imageio-ffmpeg and DeepLabCut, all installed by install_cube.bat (check with Help → System check ). A CUDA GPU: strongly recommended; CPU inference works but is very slow. Requirement Notes Step 0 files {cam_label}_{session_id}_corrected.mp4 , *_corrected_timestamps.csv and {session_id}_correction_report.json for each session Calibration recording A Charuco board recording whose session name contains "calibration", under the same source folders aniposelib Installed by install_cube.bat ; Help → System check confirms it DeepLabCut Installed by install_cube.bat , as for 2D Step 1 Group assignments, autosave, notifications, pre-processing, the Video Explorer and the Analyser work without changes. Rigs with up to three cameras and no calibration. If no calibration can be found and the rig has three or fewer cameras, Step 1b falls back to a floor-plane homography fusion of the per-camera 2D keypoints instead of stopping (see the next section and the Folders settings). A calibrated rig always triangulates in full 3D, whatever the number of cameras. Enabling 3D Mode # Add your Step 0 output folders to the main panel (the same folder list all steps use). Include the folder that holds your calibration recording's output (or its _calibration/ subfolder). Assign experimental groups if you need them; the group labels carry through to all session output. Click the 3D DLC + Anipose card (Step 1b, the alternative to 1a). Click 3D DLC Settings . Confirm that Auto-detect & auto-generate calibration.toml is ticked (the default) and enter your Charuco board's physical measurements under Charuco board geometry . Only fill in the Calibration folder field to supply a hand-made calibration.toml as a backup. Check the camera labels and any triangulation options (see 3D Settings Reference ). Click Apply & Close , then Run Step 1b . The pipeline runs unattended and sends notifications at its main milestones. Its first task is to resolve the calibration (and to calibrate automatically when needed). Clicking the Step 1b run button also switches 3D mode on; there is no separate enable checkbox in the settings. The 3D DLC + Anipose settings window: calibration, folders, camera labels and triangulation options. The Four Phases # Phase 1 — Session discovery and calibration # CUBE scans every source folder for finished Step 0 sessions. A session is a set of {cam_label}_{session_id}_corrected.mp4 files that share one session_id . A session is accepted only if at least 2 camera videos exist and every camera in the correction report has "status": "done" . Sessions are processed in order of session_id , which is chronological because it is a date and time. On a rerun, CUBE uses the source folders saved at the end of the first run, so you do not have to add them again. If the same session_id appears in several folders, the first one wins. CUBE then resolves the calibration (see Camera Calibration ). Phase 2 — Per-camera adaptation and tracking # For each camera label ( cam0 to cam3 by default), CUBE: Crops the camera's frames if you set a crop region for it. Picks a representative video: the one with the fewest duplicated frames, which shows the most genuine animal movement. Adapts the SuperAnimal Quadruped model to your recording conditions using that video. The adapted weights are cached and reused on later runs for the same camera. Tracks every corrected video of that camera. On a GPU out-of-memory error the batch size is halved and the video retried, down to a batch size of 1; if it still fails, that video is skipped and the error is logged. Masks fill frames. Frames that Step 0 marked as duplicated fill frames get a likelihood of 0 for every body point, so they cannot contribute confident detections to triangulation. Frees GPU memory before the next camera. After tracking, the calibration can be refined from the tracked keypoints (see Calibration Refinement below). This is skipped in homography fallback mode. Phase 3 — Triangulation and videos # Sessions are triangulated in parallel (up to 4 at once). For each session: Body points. Only body points present in all camera files are triangulated. If a camera lacks one, a warning is logged and that camera still contributes the points it has. Triangulation. A body point is triangulated from the cameras that see it with a likelihood above the pre-triangulation gate (default 0.4). A set of anatomical and temporal checks then removes or repairs implausible points: bone-length limits, a limit on frame-to-frame jumps, geometric priors for weakly tracked points (ears, hips, knees, nose) and a recovery step for frames seen by only one camera. RANSAC and confidence-weighted triangulation exist as options but are off by default. Confidence. The per-camera likelihoods are combined into one value per point: min (default, a point is only confident if all cameras agree, recommended for behaviour classification), mean , or max (a point is confident if any camera is). Gate. If Point confidence threshold is above 0, points below it have their likelihood set to zero and are treated as missing in Step 2. 3D file. The result is written to {session_id}_3d_filtered.h5 with the columns x , y , z and likelihood for every body point. Writing is atomic, and a session whose file already exists is skipped (so reruns are safe). A file produced by the homography fallback has no z column; if a real calibration becomes available later, it is replaced by a triangulated one, but a triangulated file is never overwritten by a fusion result. Quad video. {session_id}_quad.mp4 is a 2×2 grid of the corrected camera video
